title: Listing the chances
objectives: Build a probability mass function and check that it sums to one.
Find the chance of a set of values by adding the pmf.

screens.prose: Back to $X$, the total of two fair dice. Each cell shows its total. The cells with the same total lie on one diagonal.
screens.question: Fill in $P(X = x)$ for each total from 2 to 7. Fractions are fine.

hints.text: How many cells show a total of 2? How many show 3?
The cells with total 7 run corner to corner.
Count each diagonal: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 cells for totals 2 to 7. Put each count over 36.

feedback.correct: The chances climb by $\tfrac{1}{36}$ a step, from $\tfrac{1}{36}$ to $\tfrac{6}{36}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the cells on each total's diagonal, then divide by 36.

byKey.r0c1: A total of 2 comes from one cell: (1, 1). Divide by 36.
byKey.r1c1: A total of 3 comes from two cells: (1, 2), (2, 1). Divide by 36.
byKey.r2c1: A total of 4 comes from three cells: (1, 3), (2, 2), (3, 1). Divide by 36.
byKey.r3c1: A total of 5 comes from four cells: (1, 4), (2, 3), (3, 2), (4, 1). Divide by 36.
byKey.r4c1: A total of 6 comes from five cells: (1, 5), (2, 4), (3, 3), (4, 2), (5, 1). Divide by 36.
byKey.r5c1: A total of 7 comes from six cells: (1, 6), (2, 5), (3, 4), (4, 3), (5, 2), (6, 1). Divide by 36.

explain.text: Each chance is the number of cells on that total's diagonal, over 36. They climb by $\tfrac{1}{36}$ a step, from $\tfrac{1}{36}$ at 2 to $\tfrac{6}{36}$ at 7. Past 7 the diagonals shrink again.

screens.prose: Here is the whole list as a bar chart: one bar per total. The dashed lines are the exact chances. Roll the dice to see how real rolls compare.

state.caption: Run 1,000 rolls and compare the bars with the dashed lines

screens.question: Which total has the same chance as a total of 5?

options.why: 6 has five cells, one more than 5. Look for the bar of the same height on the other side of 7.
8 has five cells, (2, 6) to (6, 2). The chart is symmetric about 7, so 5 pairs with $14 - 5$.
10 has three cells. The bar for 5 is as tall as four cells.

hints.text: Find the bar for 5. Which bar on the other side of 7 matches it?

feedback.correct: 5 and 9 each come from four cells.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The chart is a mirror image about 7.

explain.text: Totals of 5 and 9 each come from four cells, so both have chance $\tfrac{4}{36}$. The chart is a mirror image about 7. In 1,000 rolls the bars wobble around the dashed lines.

screens.prose: Your list gives $P(X = x)$ for every value $x$ that $X$ can take. It is the **probability mass function**, or **pmf**, of $X$. We write it $p(x) = P(X = x)$.

state.caption: The pmf of the total of two dice

screens.question: Add up the whole pmf, from $p(2)$ to $p(12)$. What do you get?

hints.text: Add the cell counts first: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1.
Every one of the 36 cells has exactly one total.
The counts add to 36. Divide by 36.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the chances of all eleven totals.

byKey.half: That is $p(2)$ to $p(7)$ only, $\tfrac{21}{36}$. Totals 8 to 12 count too.
byKey.values: That counts the eleven values. Add their chances instead.
byKey.counts: That is the total number of cells. Each count is over 36, so divide.

explain.text: Every one of the 36 cells has exactly one total, so the counts add to 36 and the chances add to 1. That holds for any pmf: $X$ always takes some value. So the bars always add to 1.

screens.prose: A loaded die. Faces 1 to 5 each come up with chance 0.1. The bar for 6 is unknown. Drag the slider to set it.

derive.caption: Sum of the bars: {{fixed(values['1'] + values['2'] + values['3'] + values['4'] + values['5'] + values['6'], 2)}}

screens.question: Set $p(6)$ so that the list is a pmf.

hints.text: What must all six bars add to?
Faces 1 to 5 already use $5 \times 0.1 = 0.5$.
The bars must add to 1, so $p(6) = 1 - 0.5$.

feedback.correct: Now the six bars add to 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Watch the sum under the chart: it must read 1.00.

byKey.same: You made 6 about as likely as the other faces. Then the bars add to well under 1.
byKey.over: The bars now add to more than 1. Some chance has been counted that does not exist.
byKey.under: The bars still add to less than 1. The missing chance must go somewhere.

explain.text: Faces 1 to 5 take $0.5$ between them, so face 6 must take the other $0.5$. A pmf can be as lopsided as it likes. It only has to be non-negative and add to 1.

screens.prose: Toss a fair coin three times. Let $X$ be the number of heads. The tree lists the 8 outcomes, each with chance $\tfrac{1}{8}$.
screens.question: Fill in the pmf of $X$.

hints.text: Read the leaves. How many have no H at all?
These three leaves have exactly one head.
0 heads: TTT. 1 head: HTT, THT, TTH. 2 heads: HHT, HTH, THH. 3 heads: HHH. Put each count over 8.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the leaves with each number of heads, then divide by 8.

byKey.r0c1: Only TTT has no heads: one leaf of 8.
byKey.r1c1: One head happens three ways: HTT, THT and TTH.
byKey.r2c1: Two heads happen three ways: HHT, HTH and THH.
byKey.r3c1: Only HHH has three heads: one leaf of 8.

explain.text: One head can come on any of the three tosses, so it has three leaves. The same goes for two heads. So $p = \tfrac{1}{8}, \tfrac{3}{8}, \tfrac{3}{8}, \tfrac{1}{8}$, which adds to 1.

screens.prose: Same three tosses. Now let $S$ be the number of heads plus the number of tails.
screens.question: What is $P(S = 3)$?

hints.text: Pick any leaf. Add its heads and its tails.
HHT has 2 heads and 1 tail.
Every leaf has three tosses, so heads plus tails is always 3.

feedback.correct: $S = 3$ on every one of the 8 outcomes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out $S$ on a few leaves and compare.

byKey.one-leaf: You found one leaf with $S = 3$. Check the others: they all have $S = 3$.
byKey.zero: $S$ is never anything but 3, so $S = 3$ is certain, not impossible.

explain.text: Every leaf has three tosses, so $S = 3$ on all 8 outcomes. The pmf puts all its mass on one value: $p(3) = 1$, and $p(s) = 0$ for every other $s$. It is still a pmf, and it still adds to 1.

screens.prose: Let $N$ be the number of sixes when two dice are rolled. A classmate writes its pmf as $p(0) = \tfrac{25}{36}$, $p(1) = \tfrac{11}{36}$ and $p(2) = \tfrac{1}{36}$. Each cell with a 6 is shaded.
screens.question: Is this a valid pmf?

options.text: Yes: each chance is between 0 and 1
options.why: You checked each entry on its own. A pmf must also add to 1, and these add to $\tfrac{37}{36}$.

options.text: No: the chances add to more than 1
No: the values 0, 1 and 2 should be equally likely
options.why: You treated the values as outcomes. A pmf can be lopsided; it just has to add to 1.

hints.text: Add the three chances.
The double six is in the shaded cross. Which of $p(1)$ and $p(2)$ claims it?
$25 + 11 + 1 = 37$, so the list adds to $\tfrac{37}{36}$. The 11 cells include (6, 6), which has two sixes.

feedback.correct: The list adds to $\tfrac{37}{36}$, so something is counted twice.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add up the three chances.

byKey.yes: You checked each entry on its own. A pmf must also add to 1, and these add to $\tfrac{37}{36}$.
byKey.equal: You treated the values as outcomes. A pmf can be lopsided; it just has to add to 1.

explain.text: The 11 shaded cells have at least one six, and (6, 6) is among them. So $\tfrac{11}{36}$ counts (6, 6) in $p(1)$ as well as in $p(2)$. Exactly one six is 10 cells, $p(1) = \tfrac{10}{36}$, and then the list adds to 1.

screens.prose: Every pmf you built had the same two properties. And to find the chance of a set of values, you add their bars: $$p(x) \ge 0, \qquad \sum_x p(x) = 1, \qquad P(X \in A) = \sum_{x \in A} p(x).$$
screens.question: For the total of two dice, what is $P(X \ge 10)$? Give a fraction or a decimal.

widget.label: Chance the total is at least 10

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the bars for 10, 11 and 12.

byKey.ten-only: That is $\tfrac{3}{36}$, which leaves out some of the bars. Add all three: 10, 11 and 12.
byKey.values: You treated the eleven totals as equally likely: 3 of 11. Add their bars instead.

explain.text: $P(X \ge 10) = p(10) + p(11) + p(12) = \tfrac{3}{36} + \tfrac{2}{36} + \tfrac{1}{36} = \tfrac{1}{6}$. Any question about $X$ is a sum of bars.

screens.prose: A simple price model. Each day a share rises £2 with chance 0.3, stays flat with chance 0.5, or falls £2 with chance 0.2. Days are independent. Let $X$ be the change over two days, in £. The leaves show $X$.
screens.question: Fill in the pmf of $X$.

hints.text: Multiply along a path to get its chance: up then up is $0.3 \times 0.3$.
Three paths end at a change of 0.
$p(0) = 0.5 \times 0.5 + 0.3 \times 0.2 + 0.2 \times 0.3$. Do the same for each value, adding paths that share it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply along each path, then add the paths that end at the same change.

byKey.r1c1: Two paths give $-2$: down then flat, and flat then down. Each is $0.2 \times 0.5$.
byKey.r2c1: Three paths give 0: flat then flat, up then down, and down then up.
byKey.r3c1: Two paths give $+2$: up then flat, and flat then up. Each is $0.3 \times 0.5$.

explain.text: Each path's chance is a product, like $0.3 \times 0.5 = 0.15$ for up then flat. Paths that end at the same change add: $p(0) = 0.25 + 0.06 + 0.06 = 0.37$. The five chances add to 1, as a pmf must.

ideas: The pmf lists $p(x) = P(X = x)$ for every value $x$ that $X$ can take.
A pmf is never negative and adds to 1. If it does not, an outcome was missed or counted twice.
The chance of a set of values is the sum of their bars.

formula.name: Probability mass function
formula.note: List only values $X$ can take; every other value has $p(x) = 0$.

summary.trap: A list of chances between 0 and 1 is not enough. Add them up: $\tfrac{25}{36} + \tfrac{11}{36} + \tfrac{1}{36}$ is more than 1.

quiz.prose: A fair coin is tossed twice. $X$ is the number of heads.
quiz.question: Which list is the pmf of $X$?

options.why: You made the three values equally likely. One head happens two ways, HT and TH.
Two tosses cannot give 3 heads, and you left out 0 heads.
That adds to $\tfrac{3}{4}$. You counted one head once, but HT and TH both give it.

feedback.correct: HT and TH both give one head.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the four outcomes HH, HT, TH and TT first.

explain.text: The four outcomes HH, HT, TH and TT are equally likely. One head comes from HT and TH, so $p(1) = \tfrac{2}{4}$. The list $\tfrac{1}{4}, \tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{4}$ adds to 1.

quiz.prose: A random variable $X$ takes the values 1, 2 and 4, with $p(1) = 0.2$ and $p(2) = 0.5$.
quiz.question: What is $P(X \ge 2)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $p(4)$ first: the pmf adds to 1.

byKey.two-only: You used $p(2)$ only. $X = 4$ is also at least 2.
byKey.sum-given: You added the two chances you were given. $X = 1$ is not at least 2, and $X = 4$ is.

explain.text: The pmf adds to 1, so $p(4) = 1 - 0.2 - 0.5 = 0.3$. Then $P(X \ge 2) = p(2) + p(4) = 0.8$. Equally, it is $1 - p(1)$.

quiz.prose: Two fair dice are rolled. $Y$ is the larger of the two numbers.
quiz.question: What is $p(3) = P(Y = 3)$?

options.why: You treated the six values of $Y$ as equally likely. Count the cells whose larger die is 3.
You took all of row 3. (3, 4) has larger die 4, not 3.
That is $P(Y \le 3)$: both dice at most 3. Take away the cells where both are at most 2.

feedback.correct: Five cells have larger die exactly 3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the pairs whose larger number is exactly 3.

explain.text: The pairs are (1, 3), (2, 3), (3, 3), (3, 2) and (3, 1). That is 5 cells, so $p(3) = \tfrac{5}{36}$. Equally, $9 - 4 = 5$: both at most 3, minus both at most 2.

quiz.prose: One day of the price model: up £2 with chance 0.3, flat with chance 0.5, down £2 with chance 0.2. Let $Z = 1$ if the price rises, and $Z = 0$ otherwise.
quiz.question: What is $p(0) = P(Z = 0)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the moves that give $Z = 0$.

byKey.flat-only: You counted flat days only. A fall is not a rise either, so it also gives $Z = 0$.
byKey.down-only: You counted falls only. A flat day is not a rise either.
byKey.up: That is $P(Z = 1)$, the chance of a rise.

explain.text: $Z = 0$ on a flat day and on a fall, so $p(0) = 0.5 + 0.2 = 0.7$. And $p(1) = 0.3$. The two bars add to 1.
